name: Sofia Gubaidulina

name: Milunka Lazarević
milestone_by_age_26: Shared first place in the Yugoslav Women's Chess Championship in 1952 at age 19, and earned the Woman International Master title in 1954 at age 22.
early_history_summary: Lazarević was taught chess by her father at age 14 and quickly showed talent. She began serious study at 18 under chess instructor Zarko Popovic at the Novi Sad chess club, and by 1951 won the Serbian championship and placed second in the Yugoslav championship. In 1952 she shared first place in the Yugoslav Women's Championship.
family_context_summary: Born in the small village of Šantarovac in central Serbia; her family moved to Novi Sad. Her father and older brother played chess and taught her the game at age 14.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father and older brother played chess and introduced her to the game, providing initial domain exposure.
primary_early_advantage_tags: family chess exposure, Yugoslav chess pipeline, early competitive environment, mentor instruction
evidence_summary: Lazarević learned chess from her father at 14 and began serious study at 18 under instructor Zarko Popovic in Novi Sad. Yugoslavia was one of the strongest chess nations globally, providing a competitive ecosystem. She rose rapidly from school champion to Yugoslav Women's Championship co-winner by 1952 at age 19, and earned the WIM title in 1954 at 22. Her father and brother provided initial domain exposure, and the Yugoslav chess pipeline offered competitive opportunities.
starting_point: Born in 1932 in the small village of Šantarovac in central Serbia; her family moved to Novi Sad where her father worked. Family was of modest means.
current_position: Died on 15 December 2018 in Belgrade at age 86; remembered as one of the strongest female chess players in Yugoslav history and an 11-time national champion.

name: Jean-Pierre Jeunet
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; his short film Le manège won the César for best animated short at the 6th César Awards in February 1981 when he was 27, and his first feature film Delicatessen was released in 1991 at age 38.
early_history_summary: Jeunet bought his first camera at 17 and made short films while studying animation at Cinémation Studios. He met his longtime collaborator Marc Caro at an animation festival in Annecy in 1974. Together they made award-winning animated shorts including L'évasion (1978) and Le manège (1979), but these did not receive major recognition until the César win in 1981.
family_context_summary: Born in Roanne, in France's Loire region. He was self-taught as a filmmaker and did not attend a formal film school.
evidence_summary: Jeunet was a self-taught filmmaker who began making short films in his late teens and collaborated with Marc Caro from the mid-1970s. While he made L'évasion (1978) and Le manège (1979) before age 26, the material recognition (César Award for Le manège) came in February 1981 when he was 27. His first feature film, Delicatessen, was released in 1991 at age 38.

name: Abraham Lempel

family_context_summary: Born in 1936 in Lwów, Poland (now Lviv, Ukraine); immigrated to Israel and studied at Technion. Family background not documented in reviewed sources.

name: Vladimir Drinfeld
milestone_by_age_26: Won a gold medal with full marks at the 1969 International Mathematical Olympiad at age 15; by age 24 had defended his PhD at Moscow University and proved the Langlands conjecture for GL(2) over function fields, a landmark result in number theory.
early_history_summary: Drinfeld was a child prodigy who could do impressive mathematics by age six. He attended a specialized physics and mathematics school in Kharkov, published his first paper at 15, won IMO gold with full marks in 1969, and entered Moscow State University at 15. Under Yuri Manin's supervision, he solved a substantial part of the Langlands program by age 20 and completed the GL(2) case by age 24, defending his PhD thesis in 1978.
family_context_summary: Born into a Jewish mathematical family in Kharkov; his father Gershon Drinfeld was a mathematics professor at Kharkov University and his mother was a classical philologist.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a mathematics professor at Kharkov University who played a major role in the Kharkov Mathematical Society, providing deep mathematical immersion from childhood.
primary_early_advantage_tags: math professor father, child prodigy, specialized math school, Moscow State University, Yuri Manin mentorship, Manin seminar, IMO gold, Langlands program
evidence_summary: Drinfeld was a child prodigy born to a mathematics professor father at Kharkov University, giving him deep mathematical immersion from birth. He attended a specialized physics-mathematics school, won IMO gold with full marks at 15, and entered Moscow State University at 15. Under Yuri Manin's mentorship in the elite Algebraic Geometry Seminar, he solved a substantial part of the Langlands program by 20 and completed the GL(2) case by 24, with 13 papers in print by 1978. Despite facing anti-Semitism as a Jewish mathematician in the USSR, his extraordinary talent propelled him to a Fields Medal in 1990.
starting_point: Born in 1954 in Kharkov, Ukraine into a Jewish mathematical family; father was a mathematics professor at Kharkov University and mother was a classical philologist.
current_position: Harry Pratt Judson Distinguished Service Professor at the University of Chicago; recipient of the Fields Medal (1990), Wolf Prize (2018), and Shaw Prize (2023).

Awarded the Wolf Prize in Mathematics.

At the 1978 Miss Universe pageant in Acapulco, she was in fourth place among five finalists but won after answering the final question, becoming the first South African to win the title.

Her physical presence and the pageant pipeline provided her platform; no evidence of family domain advantage or extensive prior training was found. She later became an entertainment journalist in Los Angeles and a member of the Hollywood Foreign Press Association.
